results.result: The study employed two experimental paradigms with appropriate sample sizes and ethical approval. Ten males completed the locomotor transition experiment with two head orientations (forward and left), while six subjects (3 males, 3 females) completed the posture-to-posture transition experiment. Electrical vestibular stimulation (EVS) was applied continuously during trials, with parameters chosen based on prior literature to evoke measurable responses while ensuring subject comfort.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9, C117-C123, C133-C134 provide comprehensive methodological details that are internally consistent and well-documented. The experimental design is clearly described with appropriate sample sizes for within-subject repeated measures designs, ethical approval is documented, and EVS parameters are justified by citations to prior work. The low trial rejection rates (2.3% and 1%) indicate good data quality.

results.result: During quiet standing preceding locomotion initiation, subjects exhibited small-amplitude postural sway (shear forces: 0.39±0.3 N RMS; head acceleration: <0.01±0.3 m/s²) and significant EVS-GRF coherence across 0-10 Hz in both head orientations. Coherence peaked at 0.29±0.11 (2.1±0.6 Hz) for head forward and 0.41±0.07 (2.4±0.9 Hz) for head left conditions. At the end of quiet standing, immediately before transition onset, kinematic variables remained within the quiet standing range.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C15 present quantitative baseline measurements that establish the presence of vestibular control during quiet standing. The data are internally consistent, showing appropriate low-amplitude movements during quiet standing and significant coherence between EVS and GRF. The observation that kinematics remain stable immediately before transition (C15) is critical for establishing that the subsequent coherence drop (C16) is not due to movement onset.

results.result: EVS-GRF coherence decreased in all subjects (n=10) prior to locomotion initiation, falling below the 99% confidence limit 0.435±0.191 s before transition onset (head forward) and 0.259±0.143 s before transition (head left). This null coherence period lasted 0.860±0.260 s (head forward). The suspension began while subjects maintained quiet upright stance, well before biomechanical transition onset. This pattern was robust and observed in all 16 subjects across both experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19, C50, C54, C59, C105 collectively demonstrate the key finding of vestibular disengagement prior to movement initiation. The timing data are precise and quantitative, the effect was universal across subjects (100% showed the pattern), and the temporal relationship to biomechanical markers is clearly established. The consistency across all subjects (C59) and both experimental paradigms strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: During the transition period (head forward), EVS-GRF coherence returned, peaking at 0.18±0.05 (6.6±2.0 Hz). Coherence continued during locomotion but only during double-support phases, with first-step coherence of 0.15±0.06 (3.9±1.9 Hz). Statistical comparisons showed quiet standing coherence was significantly greater than both transition (Δ=0.17±0.10, p=0.009) and first step (Δ=0.14±0.11, p=0.012), and occurred at lower frequencies (transition: Δ=-4.4±1.9 Hz, p<0.001; first step: Δ=-4.8±1.9 Hz, p=0.015).
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C27 document the return and modulation of vestibular control after the null period. The statistical analyses are appropriate (paired t-tests with clear reporting of effect sizes and p-values), and the pattern shows context-dependent re-engagement of vestibular control. The observation of phasic modulation during gait (C21) is well-supported by the data and figures.

results.result: During locomotion termination, all subjects showed significant EVS-GRF coherence when head was forward (0.14±0.03 at 4.6±2.7 Hz) but not when head was left. Coherence was non-significant during the last double-support phase in most subjects (n=8). During the transition from locomotion to standing, coherence increased and remained significant into quiet standing, peaking at 0.41±0.08 (3.3±0.8 Hz, head forward) and 0.24±0.08 (2.4±0.4 Hz, head left). Statistical analyses confirmed last-step coherence was significantly smaller than both transition and quiet standing periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C39, C55 demonstrate vestibular disengagement also occurs at locomotion termination, beginning during the final step. The statistical comparisons are comprehensive and appropriately conducted, with consistent patterns across head orientations. The timing data (C55) shows the suspension begins during the final step and ends after transition onset, paralleling the initiation findings.

results.result: During quiet standing at the end of trials, significant EVS-GRF coherence persisted throughout, peaking at 0.43±0.09 (3.1±0.9 Hz, head forward) and 0.42±0.07 (2.0±0.5 Hz, head left). Kinematics and kinetics were similar to initial quiet standing periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 establish that vestibular control returns to baseline levels after locomotion termination. The coherence values are comparable to initial quiet standing (C13-C14), demonstrating reproducibility and supporting the interpretation that the null periods represent temporary disengagement rather than habituation or fatigue effects.

results.result: In the posture-to-posture transition experiment, subjects exhibited low-amplitude sway during initial quiet standing (<0.02±0.2 m/s², 0.44±0.4 N RMS) with significant coherence (0.45±0.21 at 3.6±1.2 Hz). Before transition onset, coherence decreased in all subjects (n=6), falling below 99% confidence 0.336±0.230 s before transition and remaining low for 0.810±0.351 s. Coherence returned during transition (0.53±0.07 at 4.7±1.9 Hz) and remained significant in the new posture (0.51±0.08 at 4.8±2.3 Hz). MANOVA showed no significant differences in peak coherence across the three phases (F(2,5)=0.76, p=0.56).
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49 demonstrate that vestibular disengagement prior to transition is not specific to locomotion initiation but represents a general phenomenon during postural transitions. The pattern mirrors the locomotor transition findings, with a pre-transition null period observed in all subjects. The statistical analysis (C49) appropriately shows that while coherence drops during the null period, the peak values before and after are similar, supporting temporary disengagement rather than permanent change.

results.result: The suspension of vestibular feedback provides evidence that balance correcting responses are down-regulated to enable transitions between motor states. This represents disengagement of one control policy prior to implementing another, supporting optimal feedback control (OFC) theory predictions. The vestibular disengagement solves the classic von Holst and Mittelstaedt problem of opposing stabilizing reflexes during motion initiation. This suppression is not specific to one transition type, suggesting a general control process. The findings demonstrate humans 'stop balancing' before moving and 'stop moving' before balancing again.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53, C56, C62-C63, C99-C104 present the primary interpretation linking experimental findings to motor control theory. The interpretation is well-supported by the consistent observation of pre-transition null periods across all subjects and both experimental paradigms. The connection to OFC theory is appropriate given the discrete temporal pattern observed. However, the interpretation remains somewhat inferential as the neural mechanisms are not directly measured.

results.result: According to optimal feedback control (OFC) theory, distinct neural processes govern posture and movement control. Transitions between motor states require disengagement of one control policy (by decreasing sensory feedback gains) prior to engaging another (by adjusting and increasing sensory feedback gains). The brain implements optimal task performance by adjusting appropriate feedback gains.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61, C106, C109-C111 accurately describe OFC theory as presented in the cited literature (Scott 2004; Cluff and Scott 2016). These are background claims establishing the theoretical framework. The citations are appropriate and the description aligns with the referenced work.

results.result: From a biomechanical perspective, vestibular disengagement may be necessary for transitions and incorporated into motor planning. The findings appear to contradict referent control theory's prediction of monotonic shifts in referent body orientation. During quiet standing, small accelerations allow adaptive feedback control with vestibular contribution. Movement initiation requires larger accelerations; unchanged vestibular gain would increase responses, potentially challenging stability. An adaptive controller must adjust vestibular gain during transitions. Results suggest gain transition is preceded by vestibular gain suppression, with context-dependent re-engagement afterward.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C74 present biomechanical and theoretical interpretations that are logical but somewhat speculative. The adaptive controller framework (C67, C70) is reasonable but not directly tested. The contradiction with referent control theory (C65) is noted but not thoroughly explored. The interpretation of gain modulation (C71-C74) is plausible given the data but represents inference rather than direct measurement of gains. These interpretations would benefit from additional experimental validation.

results.result: Significant EVS-GRF coherence was limited to 0-10 Hz despite using EVS up to 20 Hz, consistent with previous studies. Vestibular signals are low-pass filtered as they cascade from nervous system to muscle activation to whole-body accelerations. Limb and whole-body inertia impose mechanical constraints limiting frequencies at which motion can remain in phase with EVS. These low-frequency GRF responses reflect neural processing underlying organized balance correcting responses to craniocentric vestibular error signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 explain the frequency characteristics of the observed responses. The observations (C77) are clearly documented in the data. The interpretation is well-supported by citations to prior work (C78-C79) and biomechanical principles (C80). The mechanistic explanation (C81) is reasonable and supported by the cited literature, though it remains somewhat inferential regarding the specific neural processing involved.

results.result: Primary motor cortex neurons show task-specific responses to mechanical loads, active only during posture maintenance or movement. Kurtzer et al. (2005) observed abrupt neural processing switches ~0.3 s before posture-to-reaching transitions. The current results mirror this behavior and extend the framework to balance-locomotor contexts. Brainstem selective attenuation of 'vestibular only' neurons might contribute but would be ineffective at suppressing unpredictable EVS signals. Recent findings indicate this mechanism is likely insufficient to explain the observed vestibular-evoked response suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 appropriately contextualize findings within neurophysiological literature. The comparison to Kurtzer et al. (C83-C84) is apt given the similar temporal patterns (~0.3 s pre-transition). The discussion of brainstem mechanisms (C85-C87) appropriately acknowledges potential contributions while noting limitations based on recent work. The interpretation is balanced and well-supported by citations.

results.result: EVS-evoked responses are craniocentric, allowing directional manipulation via head orientation. During locomotion, frontal plane posture is unstable (center of mass medial to propulsive foot) while sagittal plane stability is enhanced by forward momentum and long base of support during double-support. This stability difference may explain small/absent vestibular responses when head is turned left (anteroposterior direction). Reduced EVS-anteroposterior GRF coherence supports the hypothesis that anteroposterior balance during locomotion requires less feedback-driven control and may be largely passively controlled. Vestibular-evoked whole-body responses in the frontal plane are phasically modulated during locomotion, with larger coherence during double-support phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C98 explain the head orientation effects observed in the data. The biomechanical explanations (C89-C90, C96) are well-established and appropriately cited. The interpretation linking stability differences to vestibular response patterns (C91-C93) is logical and supported by the data showing minimal coherence in the head-left condition during walking. The observation of phasic modulation (C94) is clearly demonstrated in the figures and extends prior single-muscle findings to whole-body responses.

results.result: The vestibular system encodes head motion and is vital for maintaining stability during quiet standing and locomotion. Vestibular signals influence postural muscle activation in a context-dependent manner, depending on muscles' engagement in balance control and alignment with the plane of instability and vestibular disturbance direction. Contextually-dependent vestibular responses occur during both quiet standing and locomotion, with magnitude modulated by gait cycle phase.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 present well-established background knowledge about vestibular function, appropriately supported by multiple citations to authoritative sources spanning several decades. These claims provide essential context for the study but represent prior knowledge rather than novel findings.

results.result: Inhibition of ankle plantar flexor activity during locomotion initiation occurs 150 ms before the first vertical GRF change, suggesting balance correcting responses are down-regulated 100-300 ms before step-related muscle activity modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 appropriately cite prior work (Herman et al., 1973) and use it to contextualize the current timing findings. The inference about timing of down-regulation (C58) is reasonable given both the cited work and current findings, though it involves some extrapolation.

results.result: An alternative interpretation is that the brain abruptly switches policies and begins predicting the whole-body's future state while the body remains in the previous state. This would create a temporary discrepancy between predicted and actual sensory feedback, potentially reducing vestibular-evoked response size.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 present a speculative alternative interpretation. While this predictive coding explanation is plausible and cited (Luu et al., 2012), it is not directly tested and remains hypothetical. The authors appropriately present it as an alternative rather than a definitive explanation, but it lacks direct experimental support in the current study.

results.result: Movement initiation from stable posture is a central neuroscience issue due to the need to overcome reflex-stabilizing mechanisms. Balance correcting responses may hinder locomotor initiation and transitions. Referent control theory suggests transitions involve monotonic shifts in referent body orientation, transforming posture-stabilizing mechanisms into movement-inducing ones.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108, C112-C113 present established background on the motor control problem being addressed and alternative theoretical frameworks. The citations are appropriate (von Holst and Mittelstaedt 1950; Ostry and Feldman 2003; Feldman et al. 2011; Mullick et al. 2018) and accurately represent the cited work.

results.result: EVS non-specifically modulates vestibular nerve firing rates and, in binaural bipolar configuration, evokes rotation perception about an axis 18° posteriorly and superiorly from Reid's plane. With head forward, EVS induces frontal plane postural responses; with head turned 90° left, responses are in the anteroposterior plane. Support width influences EVS-evoked response magnitude.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116, C124-C126 describe well-established properties of EVS, appropriately supported by multiple citations. These are methodological background claims that justify the experimental approach. The characterization is accurate and consistent with the cited literature.

results.result: Comparing trials with and without EVS in the locomotor transition experiment revealed no major behavioral differences except at locomotion termination, where EVS trials showed significantly decreased transition periods (head forward: Δ=-0.094±0.070 s, p<0.001; head left: Δ=-0.330±0.123 s, p<0.001) and increased walking velocity (head forward: Δ=0.044±0.013 m/s, p<0.001; head left: Δ=0.113±0.070 m/s, p<0.001). No significant behavioral differences were found in the posture-to-posture experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C132 document control analyses comparing EVS and no-EVS trials. The statistical analyses are appropriate and clearly reported. The finding that EVS had minimal effects on behavior (except small effects at termination) supports the validity of using EVS as a probe without substantially altering the motor task. However, the significant effects at termination (C128-C131) suggest EVS does have some behavioral impact that should be considered when interpreting those results.

results.result: Subjects reached their preferred locomotion speed on average after the second step.
results.evaluation: Claim C135 cites prior work (Jian et al., 1993) to justify the walking distance used in the experimental design. This is appropriate use of prior literature to support methodological choices.
